hook.situation: A Korean colleague invites you for samgyeopsal tonight. You want to go, you probably can go — but you're not sure yet. In English you'd say 'I want to go,' 'I can go,' or 'I can't go.' Korean has three distinct grammar forms for these three meanings, and mixing them up sounds strange: saying 못 가고 싶어요 (a nonsensical blend) signals confusion between wanting and being able.
objectives: Use 고 싶어요 correctly to express what you want or desire to do
Use ㄹ/을 수 있어요 to say you can do something (ability or possibility)
Use 못 + verb to say you cannot do something — and know why 못 가해요 is wrong
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns are the engine of polite Korean conversation. Koreans use them constantly to navigate invitations, menus, schedules, and apologies. Without them you can only say what you DO — you can't express what you want, what you're capable of, or what you have to decline. Master all three and you can have real adult conversations about your life.

grammarNotes.title: 고 싶어요 — Expressing Desire (I want to...)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 고 싶어요 as a MAGNET. The verb stem is pulling you toward an action — something attracts you, something you haven't done yet but are drawn to do. The magnet doesn't move by itself; it expresses the pull. 싶다 literally means 'to feel drawn to' — it always attaches to the verb stem + 고, never to a noun.

examples.note: 마시다 → stem 마시 + 고 싶어요. The magnet pulls you toward drinking coffee — you haven't drunk it yet.

examples.en: I want to go to Korea.
examples.note: 가다 → stem 가 + 고 싶어요. A desire about a future movement — the magnet pulls you toward Korea.

examples.en: I want to eat food that isn't spicy.
examples.note: 먹다 → stem 먹 + 고 싶어요. Practical desire at a restaurant — key real-life use of this form.

examples.en: I want to speak Korean well.
examples.note: 하다 → stem 하 + 고 싶어요. A longer-term aspiration, not just an immediate craving — 고 싶어요 covers both.
쉬다 → stem 쉬 + 고 싶어요. The stem keeps its final vowel; no consonant changes needed here.

contrastPairs.explanation: Same action, very different meaning. 고 싶어요 = internal desire, a pull toward the action. 먹을 수 있어요 = capability or circumstantial possibility. A vegetarian might say 먹을 수 있어요 (physically capable) but not 먹고 싶어요 (no desire). A sick person might say 먹고 싶어요 (wants to) but not 먹을 수 있어요 (can't right now).

a.en: I want to watch a movie. (desire)

contrastPairs.explanation: These can both be true at the same time! You can want to do something and be unable to do it. 고 싶어요 is about your desire; 못 봐요 is about whether the action is possible. Together: 영화를 보고 싶은데 못 봐요 — I want to watch a movie but can't.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English says 'I want coffee' with just a noun. Korean 싶다 attaches to a VERB, not a noun — you can't say 커피를 싶어요. You must always say what you want to DO: 마시고 싶어요 (want to drink). For nouns use 원해요 or rephrase: 커피 한 잔 주세요 (please give me a coffee) — but 고 싶어요 always needs a verb stem before it.

exceptions: 고 싶다 describes the speaker's own desire. To say 'Minho wants to go,' use 가고 싶어해요 (third person shows desire as observed behavior), not 가고 싶어요.
Past desire: 가고 싶었어요 = I wanted to go (but didn't / past feeling).
Negative desire: 가고 싶지 않아요 = I don't want to go (more direct than 못 가요, which means can't).

grammarNotes.title: ㄹ/을 수 있어요 & 못 — Ability and Inability
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Picture a DOOR. 수 있어요 is an open door — you CAN walk through; the path is clear. 못 is a locked door — the way is blocked, whether by circumstance, rule, or physical impossibility. The key difference from English: 못 is a pre-verb blocker (it goes BEFORE the verb), not a separate sentence ending.
grammarNotes.formation: Ability: Verb stem + ㄹ/을 수 있어요 (stem ends in vowel → ㄹ 수, ends in consonant → 을 수) | Inability: 못 + plain verb (present tense)

examples.en: I can go to the café today.
examples.note: 가다 → stem 가 (ends in vowel) → 갈 수 있어요. Open door: the possibility exists today.
먹다 → stem 먹 (ends in consonant ㄱ) → 먹을 수 있어요. Stating ability: I'm capable of eating spicy food.

examples.en: I can speak a little Korean.
examples.note: 하다 → stem 하 (ends in vowel) → 할 수 있어요. Modest ability claim — very useful for newcomers.
못 blocks 가요 from the front. Notice: 못 가요, NOT 못 가해요 — 가다 is not a 하다-verb so no 해요 added.
못 + 마셔요. A real-life sentence for politely declining alcohol — essential for daily life in Korea.

b.en: I can't go. (blocked — circumstance or rule)

contrastPairs.explanation: Both mean inability but with a slight nuance. 갈 수 없어요 = the possibility doesn't exist (like a road is closed). 못 가요 = something is blocking it — often external circumstances, schedules, or physical restrictions. In conversation, 못 가요 feels more natural and casual; 갈 수 없어요 sounds a bit more formal or definitive.

b.en: I can't speak Korean. (inability — 하다 verb!)

contrastPairs.explanation: 하다 verbs are special with 못: 못 해요 (not 못 하해요). The 하 merges with 못: 한국어를 못 해요. Compare 못 가요 (for 가다) — no extra 해요. This is the #1 mistake beginners make with 못.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 한국어를 못 해요. / 한국어를 못 말해요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Actually both forms exist — 못 말해요 (can't speak/say) and 못 해요 (can't do it) are both grammatically fine. The real pitfall is 못 가해요 for 가다: learners wrongly apply the 하다 pattern to regular verbs. 가다 is NOT a 하다 verb, so 못 가요 is correct, 못 가해요 is wrong. Only 하다 verbs (공부하다, 운동하다, 전화하다) use 못 해요.

exceptions: 하다 verbs with 못: 공부 못 해요, 운동 못 해요, 전화 못 해요 — the 하다 part becomes 해요, and 못 goes before the whole expression or between the noun and 해요.
ㄹ irregular in 수 있어요: 알다 → 알 수 있어요 (not 알을 수 있어요); 만들다 → 만들 수 있어요.
살다 (to live) → 살 수 있어요 (the ㄹ already ends the stem — just add 수 있어요).

exampleSentence.en: I want to eat something that isn't spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 먹고 싶어요 — desire form; essential at Korean restaurants for dietary preferences
마시 + 고 싶어요 — the stem ends in a vowel so 고 attaches cleanly

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 내일 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: Two patterns in one sentence: 못 가요 (blocked today) vs 갈 수 있어요 (open tomorrow)

exampleSentence.en: I want to speak Korean well.
exampleSentence.note: 하 + 고 싶어요 — long-term aspiration; note that 못 for 하다 = 못 해요, NOT 못 하해요
말하다 → stem 말하 + ㄹ 수 있어요 → 말할 수 있어요; often used to express language ability

extendedVocabulary.english: to be able to eat / can eat

exampleSentence.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.note: 먹 (consonant ending stem) + 을 수 있어요 — consonant stems take 을 수, vowel stems take ㄹ 수

exampleSentence.ko: 이 음식은 너무 매워서 못 먹어요.
exampleSentence.en: This food is too spicy so I can't eat it.
exampleSentence.note: 맵다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 매워서 (not 맵어서) — important for describing food limitations

exampleSentence.en: It's okay even if it's a little spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 괜찮아요 alone works as 'it's fine'; combined with 먹을 수 있어요 context it reassures the other person
알다 is ㄹ-irregular: 알 + 아요 = 알아요. For ability: 알 수 있어요 (stem already ends in ㄹ so no extra ㄹ added)

exampleSentence.en: Can you come to the party today?
exampleSentence.note: 오다 → stem 오 (vowel) → 올 수 있어요? A common social question — the ㄹ is added to the vowel stem

exampleSentence.en: I want to rest a bit today.
exampleSentence.note: 쉬 + 고 싶어요 — expressing the very human desire for rest; common in daily conversation

exampleSentence.en: Lately I'm busy so I can't exercise.
exampleSentence.note: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb: 못 + 해요 = 못 해요. The noun 운동 and 못 해요 can be separated: 운동 못 해요.

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘 시간이 있어요? 같이 밥 먹고 싶어요.
exampleSentence.en: Do you have time today? I want to eat together.
exampleSentence.note: 시간이 있어요 is the natural Korean way to say 'have time' — pairs perfectly with 고 싶어요 for invitations

exampleSentence.en: I'm too busy today so I can't go.
exampleSentence.note: 바쁘다 is ㅡ-irregular: 바빠서 (not 바쁘어서). Used constantly as a reason for 못 + verb

exampleSentence.en: What do you want to order?
exampleSentence.note: 주문하 + 고 싶어요 — essential restaurant phrase; 주문하다 is a 하다 verb

exampleSentence.ko: 아직 한국어를 다 이해할 수 없어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't understand all Korean yet.
exampleSentence.note: 이해하다 → 이해할 수 없어요 — a humble and accurate self-assessment for language learners

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 다음에 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go next time.
exampleSentence.note: 못 always goes BEFORE the verb. It's not a sentence ending — it's a pre-verb blocker. 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 못 마셔요.

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihye invites her coworker Minsu to dinner at a Korean BBQ restaurant

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 민수 씨, 오늘 저녁에 삼겹살 먹고 싶지 않아요?
lines.romanization: Minsu ssi, oneul jeonyeoge samgyeopsal meokgo sipji anhayo?
lines.en: Minsu, don't you want to eat samgyeopsal this evening?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶지 않아요? — negative form of 먹고 싶어요, used as a soft invitation. Literally 'don't you want to eat?' — gentler than a direct 먹고 싶어요?

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 네, 먹고 싶어요! 어디에서 먹을 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Ne, meokgo sipeoyo! Eodiese meogeul su isseoyo?
lines.en: Yes, I want to eat it! Where can we eat it?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶어요 (desire) + 먹을 수 있어요 (possibility) — two separate patterns in two sentences. 먹 ends in a consonant so 을 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 회사 근처에 좋은 식당이 있어요. 7시에 갈 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Hoesa geuncheoe joeun sikdangi isseoyo. Ilgop-ssie gal su isseoyo?
lines.en: There's a good restaurant near the office. Can you go at 7?
lines.grammarNote: 갈 수 있어요? — open-door question: is your door open at 7? 가다 stem 가 (vowel) → 갈 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 7시는 좀... 오늘 회의가 있어서 6시까지 못 가요.
lines.romanization: Ilgop-ssineun jom... oneul hoeuiga isseoseo yeoseot-ssikkaji mot gayo.
lines.en: 7 o'clock is a bit... I have a meeting today so I can't go until 6.
lines.grammarNote: 못 가요 — locked door: the meeting blocks him. 못 directly precedes the verb stem 가요. Note: NOT 못 가해요.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.en: Then how about 8 o'clock? I can wait.
lines.grammarNote: 기다릴 수 있어요 — 기다리다 stem 기다리 (vowel) → 기다릴 수 있어요. She's reassuring him by stating her own capability to wait.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 감사해요! 그런데 저는 너무 매운 것은 못 먹어요.
lines.romanization: Gamsahaeyo! Geureonde jeoneun neomu maeun geoseun mot meogeoyo.
lines.en: Thank you! But I can't eat things that are too spicy.
lines.grammarNote: 못 먹어요 — locked door for spicy food: a dietary limitation. This is 못 + 먹어요 (plain verb form). Useful for communicating food restrictions.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 거기서 맵지 않은 것도 먹을 수 있어요.
lines.romanization: Gwaenchanhayo. Geogiseo maepji aneun geotdo meogeul su isseoyo.
lines.en: That's okay. You can also eat non-spicy things there.
lines.grammarNote: 먹을 수 있어요 — open door: the possibility exists. 먹 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을 수 있어요. She's reassuring with an ability/option statement.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.romanization: Wanjeon joayo! Yeodeol-ssie sikdang apeseo mannayo.
lines.en: Sounds perfect! Let's meet in front of the restaurant at 8.
lines.grammarNote: No grammar notes needed — 만나요 is a Chapter 6 review. Notice how want (먹고 싶어요), can (먹을 수 있어요), and can't (못 먹어요) all appeared naturally in this conversation.

readingText.title: 단체 채팅방 — 이번 주말에 뭐 할 수 있어요? (Group Chat — What can everyone do this weekend?)
readingText.body:
지은: 이번 주말에 같이 한강에 가고 싶어요. 다들 어때요?
유진: 저도 가고 싶어요! 토요일에 갈 수 있어요.
다니엘: 저는 토요일에 일이 있어서 못 가요. 일요일은 갈 수 있어요.
지은: 그럼 일요일에 가요! 자전거도 탈 수 있어요?
유진: 저는 자전거를 탈 수 있어요. 재미있겠다!
다니엘: 저는 자전거를 잘 못 타요. 천천히 가도 돼요?
지은: 물론이죠! 천천히 가고 싶은 사람도 있어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jieun: I want to go to the Han River together this weekend. What does everyone think?
Yujin: I want to go too! I can go on Saturday.
Daniel: I have work on Saturday so I can't go. I can go on Sunday.
Jieun: Then let's go on Sunday! Can you also ride bikes?
Yujin: I can ride a bike. That sounds fun!
Daniel: I can't ride a bike well. Is it okay if we go slowly?
Jieun: Of course! There are also people who want to go slowly.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why can't Daniel go on Saturday?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 일이 있어서 못 가요 — he has work, so something is blocking him (못 = locked door).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Daniel say about bike riding, and how does he express it?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 자전거를 잘 못 타요 — he can't ride a bike well. He uses 못 before 타요 (ride) to express inability. 잘 못 = 'not well' (not exactly the same as 전혀 못 = 'can't at all').

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 고 싶어요, ㄹ/을 수 있어요, and 못 in the text. For each one, identify which grammar pattern it is and explain why that specific pattern is used instead of the others.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 고 싶어요 (desire): 한강에 가고 싶어요 (Jieun wants to go — her desire), 저도 가고 싶어요 (Yujin shares the desire), 천천히 가고 싶은 사람도 있어요 (people who want to go slowly — desire modifier). | 수 있어요 (ability/possibility): 토요일에 갈 수 있어요 (Yujin: the door is open Saturday), 일요일은 갈 수 있어요 (Daniel: Sunday door is open), 자전거도 탈 수 있어요? (is the door open for biking?), 자전거를 탈 수 있어요 (Yujin: yes, open door). | 못 (inability): 토요일에 못 가요 (Daniel: work blocks Saturday — locked door), 자전거를 잘 못 타요 (Daniel: skill gap blocks him).

culturalNote.title: 못 해요 as the polite Korean refusal
culturalNote.body: In Korean social culture, saying you 'can't' do something (못 해요) is often more polite and face-saving than saying you 'don't want to' (싶지 않아요). If someone invites you somewhere you don't want to go, saying 오늘 못 가요 (I can't go today) is a softer decline than 가고 싶지 않아요 (I don't want to go), which can sound blunt or even rude. This is why Koreans sometimes use 못 해요 even when the real reason is lack of desire, not inability. When you start hearing 못 해요 in Korean conversations, know that it often carries the social function of a gentle 'no' — not necessarily a factual statement about impossibility.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 초밥을 먹___ 싶어요. (I want to eat sushi.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 고 싶어요 requires 고 between the verb stem and 싶어요. The stem of 먹다 is 먹, so: 먹고 싶어요. 을 would start the ability form (먹을 수 있어요), and 는 is a topic marker — neither makes sense here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘 회의가 있어서 ___ 가요. (I can't go because I have a meeting today.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 expresses inability blocked by circumstances (the meeting). 안 가요 = 'I don't go / I won't go' (choice or habit, not inability). 고 싶지 않아요 = 'I don't want to go' (lack of desire). Only 못 captures 'I'm blocked — I can't.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '운동을 못 가해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb. The 못 inability form for 하다 verbs is 못 해요 — NOT 못 가해요 (that mixes in 가다 for no reason) and NOT 못 하해요 (that doubles the verb). The noun and 못 해요 can be split: 운동 못 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I can speak a little Korean.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 말할 수 있어요 = ability/capability (open door). Option A (말하고 싶어요) = 'I want to speak Korean' — that's desire, not ability. Option C (못 말해요) = 'I can't speak Korean' — the opposite of what you want to say. For expressing language ability, ㄹ/을 수 있어요 is the right tool.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I want to rest today, but I can't.'
inlineExercises.correct: 오늘 쉬고 싶어요. 그런데 못 쉬어요.
inlineExercises.hint: You need two patterns: 쉬다 (to rest) with 고 싶어요 for desire, and 못 + verb for inability. The two parts contrast with 그런데 (but/however).

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 매운 음식을 먹___ 수 있어요. (I can eat spicy food.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹다 has a consonant-ending stem (먹, ending in ㄱ). Consonant-ending stems take 을 수 있어요, not ㄹ 수 있어요. ㄹ 수 attaches to vowel-ending stems (가 → 갈 수, 오 → 올 수). 고 would start the desire form — not ability.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your Korean friend says '술 마시고 싶어요?' You can't drink alcohol. What's the most natural reply?
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 마셔요 is the most natural, socially smooth way to decline — it signals inability/circumstances rather than personal rejection, which is more polite in Korean culture. 마시고 싶지 않아요 (don't want to) sounds blunt. 마실 수 없어요 is grammatically fine but sounds formal/stiff in casual conversation. 못 마셔요 is the everyday go-to for dietary or health limitations.

bullets: MAGNET (고 싶어요): Verb stem + 고 싶어요 = desire, a pull toward an action. Always needs a verb — you can't attach it to a noun.
OPEN DOOR (ㄹ/을 수 있어요): Vowel stem + ㄹ 수 있어요 / Consonant stem + 을 수 있어요 = ability or possibility. The path is clear.
LOCKED DOOR (못 + verb): 못 goes BEFORE the regular verb form. For 하다 verbs: 못 해요, never 못 가해요 or 못 하해요.
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 9 introduces 아/어서 and 그래서 — connectors that let you give REASONS for your wants, abilities, and inabilities. You'll finally be able to say not just 'I can't go' but 'I can't go because I'm busy.'
